newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Billiton makes confident start as true Brit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Billiton makes confident start as true Brit.

text.p: South African mining house Billiton on Monday set out plans to become one of Britain's leading companies, with its sights set firmly on entering the FTSE 100 index of leading companies later this year.
Billiton is being demerged from its South African parent Gencor Ltd, which intends to concentrate on mining precious metals.

Billiton, one of the world's biggest producers of aluminium, nickel and coal, said it expected to be valued at between 4.4 billion and 5.1 billion pounds ($8.6 billion) when its shares start trading on July 23, with a target price of between 210 pence and 240 pence per share.
Analysts expect the flotation to be well received, despite concerns over other South African mining houses.
"Overall it's a quality company," said one analyst with a London brokerage. "It will generate strong cash flow and growth in a sector that will grow on the back of world (economic) expansion."
With a place in the FTSE 100 likely in the autumn, Billiton can expect strong support from British institutional shareholders, analysts said.
Gencor acquired Billiton from Royal Dutch Shell for $1.2 billion in 1994. As well as extensive operations in South Africa, the company operates in South America, Australia and Canada.

Billiton, which has established its head office at that most British of addresses on The Strand in London, a piece of coal's throw from South Africa House, did not hide the commercial advantages it expects to flow from becoming a British-based business.

"We need to access international capital to continue (our) record of growth," chairman and chief executive officer Brian Gilbertson said. "South Africa's foreign exchange controls have proved a significant handicap to our ambitions."

Gilbertson said increased financial muscle would allow Billiton to take advantage of opportunities as they arose around the world. "The balance sheet is robust with substantial debt capacity," he added.

The company's focus will be on expanding and improving production at existing operations, and taking advantage of a number of planned mining privatisations in countries including Venezuela, Colombia and Brazil.

One major headache for Billiton, last week's decision by British finance minister Gordon Brown to abolish foreign income dividends from 1999, seemed to have eased after assurances from the British government.

Brown said last week he wanted to end the system under which companies could avoid being taxed in Britain on earnings made and taxed abroad which were then distributed as dividends. This would be a particular problem for Billiton which will make almost all its earnings outside the UK.
However, chief financial officer Mick Davis said he had been assured by the government that the "problems will be resolved."
One reservation being expressed about Billiton on Monday was its exposure to the wobbly South African rand.

An analyst with a European bank in London said this was likely to mean Billiton would trade at a discount to its giant rival Rio Tinto Plc of around 15 percent on a price/earnings relative. Rio Tinto was trading on a p/e relative of just under 21 on Monday according to Reuters 3000 data.
Billiton said it expected attributable profits of at least $330 million in the year ended June 30, 1997, giving an earnings per share figure of 19.3 cents.
